world.bio: Australian from Perth working the broth station at a small ramen shop in Koenji, Tokyo. I am the only foreigner in the kitchen. Eighteen months in on a working holiday visa that ends next spring. I make tonkotsu and shoyu broths, wake at 6am to start the pork bones, and cycle along the Zenpukuji river on days off. Homesick for Perth beaches most of the time.
skills_assets: Tonkotsu broth: 14-hour pork bone simmer, manages two 60-litre pots
Kitchen Japanese at about N4 level, restaurant vocabulary only
Perth hospitality network: two former head chefs who rate him
A beat-up road bike bought secondhand in Nakano
Instagram account with 900 followers, mostly broth photos
Valid Australian driver licence, Japanese international permit

projects.name: Broth consistency log
projects.text: Keeping a notebook of every batch: bone weight, water, simmer time, ambient temperature, the boss's tasting notes. After eighteen months I can finally predict why the Tuesday batch always tastes thinner. Might turn this into something one day.

projects.name: Apartment renewal
projects.text: Landlord's agent emailed a renewal contract, three pages entirely in formal keigo Japanese. I put it through a translator and some clauses look odd (a renewal fee, a cleaning fee, something about a guarantor company). I am afraid to sign something I cannot read.

projects.name: Cycling the Tamagawa
projects.text: Want to ride the whole Tamagawa cycling road, 50 km each way, before the winter.

notes.text: Up at 5:40. Pork bones in the pot by 6:15. Boss said the broth looked 'sunao', meaning honest. I think it's a compliment. Still not sure.

Day off. Rode from Koenji to the Zenpukuji park and back. Fed the carp. Thinking about the sea at Cottesloe, how the water goes clear in March. Bought a can of Milo at the import shop and drank it standing in the aisle.

Agent emailed the renewal contract. Three pages of keigo. The words I know: contract, rent, deposit. The rest looks like a wall. Translator says 'renewal fee of one month's rent' and 'the lessee shall pay' something to a guarantor company. I don't know if this is normal.
Asked coworker Tanaka-san about the contract. He said it's probably standard, but he's never rented a place himself because he lives with his mum. Thanks mate.
Long shift, 13 hours. Feet are bricks. The boss gave me an onigiri and said, quietly, 'gambatte'. I almost cried over a rice ball.
Called my mate Jack in Perth. It was 6pm there and he was on the beach. He said come home. I said I can't, I only just started to be good at this.
Visa ends in April. Do I try to switch to a work visa? Need a sponsor, and the boss said he'll think about it. He says that about everything.
The renewal deadline is October 20. If I don't sign they might ask me to leave. I keep opening the PDF and closing it.
Went to a free English-Japanese exchange night in Shinjuku. Met a girl who studies Korean. We swapped phrases. She laughed at my keigo.

messages.text:
Kobayashi: Liam, tomorrow, stock early.
Me: Hai, 5:30.
Kobayashi: Good.

Yamada: ご契約更新のご案内をお送りいたします。
Me: Thank you. I will read it.
Yamada: 期限は10月20日です。
Me: (checks translator) October 20, ok.

Mum: Is everything alright, love? You sound tired.
Me: Just long shifts.
Mum: Don't forget to eat vegetables.
Me: I eat ramen every day, Mum.

Jack: Waves are firing today.
Me: Send a photo.
Jack: [photo]
Me: I hate you.

Tanaka: Liam, are you free Sunday? Fishing?
Me: Yes please.
Tanaka: Bring a cap.

relations.about: Fifty-eight, thirty years at the stove, speaks little, kind in small gestures.
Twenty-six, lives with his mum, helpful but cannot help with housing.
Perth surf buddy, keeps telling him to come home.

constraints: Working holiday visa ends next spring, no long commitments
Shifts run from 6am to 9pm, little time for paperwork
Cannot afford a lawyer or a paid agent
Japanese reading is poor, will not sign what he cannot understand
sensitive: Terrified of being scammed or evicted in a country where he cannot read the paper
Homesick enough to cry sometimes in the walk-in fridge
